# 2 Samuel Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 179v–180r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_011_page_001.jpg, 2SA_011_page_002.jpg

---

**1** In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent Joab out with his officers and the whole Israelite army. They devastated the Ammonites and laid siege to Rabbah. But David stayed behind in Jerusalem.

**2** One evening David got up from his couch and was walking on the roof of the palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing — and she was strikingly beautiful. **3** David sent someone to find out about her. The report came back: "She is Bathsheba daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite."

**4** David sent messengers to get her. She came to him, and he slept with her. (She had just completed her ritual purification after her monthly period.) Then she went back home.

**5** The woman discovered she was pregnant. She sent word to David: "I am with child."

**6** David sent a message to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." So Joab sent Uriah to David.

**7** When Uriah arrived, David asked him how Joab was doing, how the troops were, and how the war was going. **8** Then David said to Uriah, "Go on home and wash your feet." When Uriah left the palace, the king sent a gift after him. **9** But Uriah slept at the palace entrance with all his master's servants. He did not go home.

**10** When David was told, "Uriah didn't go home," David said to him, "Haven't you just come from a long march? Why didn't you go home?"

**11** Uriah replied, "The ark, and Israel, and Judah are all out there living in tents. My commander Joab and my lord's troops are camped in the open field. How could I go home and eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live — I swear on your very life — I will never do such a thing."

**12** David said, "Stay here one more day. Tomorrow I'll send you back." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.

**13** David invited him to eat and drink with him, and got him drunk. But that evening Uriah went out and slept on his mat among his master's servants. He still would not go home.

**14** The next morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah himself.

**15** The letter said: "Put Uriah at the front where the fighting is fiercest. Then pull back and leave him exposed, so that he will be struck down and killed."

**16** While Joab had the city under siege, he placed Uriah at a point where he knew the toughest enemy fighters were stationed. **17** The defenders came out and attacked Joab's forces. Some of David's men fell in the fighting, and Uriah the Hittite was among the dead.

**18** Joab sent David a full report of the battle. **19** He told the messenger, "When you've finished giving the king the whole battle report, **20** if the king gets angry and asks, 'Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Didn't you know they'd shoot from the wall? **21** Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Wasn't it a woman who dropped a millstone on him from the wall at Thebez? Why did you go near the wall?' — then say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.'"

**22** The messenger went to David and delivered everything Joab had sent him to say. **23** He told David, "Their men were getting the better of us — they came out into the open against us, but we pushed them back to the city gate. **24** Then the archers on the wall shot down at your men. Some of the king's soldiers died — and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."

**25** David told the messenger, "Say this to Joab: 'Don't let this upset you — the sword cuts down one man as easily as another. Press your attack against the city and level it.' Tell him to keep his spirits up."

**26** When Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him.

**27** After the period of mourning, David had her brought to his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "But David stayed behind":** The narrator drops this sentence like a stone into still water. The entire chapter flows from it. Kings go out. David stays. Five words of absence that open the door to adultery, deception, and murder.

**Verse 4 — the parenthetical:** The narrator inserts a clinical note — she was purifying herself from her period — into the middle of an act of royal power. Its coldness is deliberate. It tells us two things at once: she was bathing for religious reasons (not seduction), and the child can only be David's. The precision of the note is the narrator's quiet devastation.

**Verse 11 — Uriah's speech:** Uriah is everything David should be: loyal, principled, aware of the covenant. He will not go home to comfort while the ark and the army are in the field. The irony cuts to bone — this foreign soldier is more faithful to Israel's God and Israel's covenant than the king himself. And the oath — "I swear on your very life" — is unbearable once you know what David is planning.

**Verse 14 — the letter in Uriah's hand:** This is perhaps the most devastating verse in the Hebrew Bible for what it does *not* say. Uriah, the loyal soldier who refused even to wash his feet at home, now carries his own death sentence back to the front. The narrator does not tell us if the letter was sealed, if Uriah wondered about its contents, if he had any suspicion. The silence is the cruelty.

**Verse 25 — "the sword cuts down one man as easily as another":** David has become a man who can shrug off the murder of a loyal soldier with a proverb about the randomness of war. He has reduced Uriah's death to a statistic. The verb "devours" (in the Hebrew) personifies the sword as an appetite that cannot be blamed — as if war, not David, killed Uriah. This is the language of a man who has taught himself not to feel.

**Verse 27 — the verdict:** Throughout this chapter, the narrator has been icily restrained, reporting monstrous acts in flat, factual prose. No commentary, no adjectives, no condemnation — until now. "But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD." One sentence. The silence breaks. And the next chapter will bring the reckoning.

*— PNEUMA*
